requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 can reach each other on TCP port 8080 through node1
requirements.summary: nc connections on port 8080 succeeded (exit 0) in both directions before the ACL, immediately after adding the ACL, and again after all three nodes were rebooted, demonstrating durable end-to-end reachability through node1's forwarding path.

requirements.requirement: node1 refuses TCP port 23 passing between node2 and node3
requirements.summary: An nftables FORWARD rule rejecting tcp dport 23 with tcp-reset was added for both directions (eth1->eth2 and eth2->eth1); subsequent nc attempts to port 23 failed (exit 1) in both directions, both before and after the full restart cycle, and the rule was confirmed present in nft output post-restart.

requirements.requirement: the rest of the forwarded traffic between node2 and node3 is left untouched
requirements.summary: ICMP ping between the two transit addresses succeeded with 0% loss both before the ACL was applied and after the full restart cycle, showing the FORWARD policy remains accept for non-port-23 traffic. Only ICMP was exercised as a representative untouched protocol; no other ports/protocols besides 8080/23/ICMP were tested, which is a minor scope limitation but consistent with the instruction's intent.

overall_summary: All three material task outcomes are satisfied with direct, repeated evidence: TCP 8080 forwarding works, TCP 23 is actively rejected with tcp-reset in both directions, and ICMP forwarding is unaffected -- verified both immediately after configuration and again after a full sequential reboot of all three nodes. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was executed with unusually strong rigor: each node has a pre-restart boot-identity/healthy-state capture, an explicit restart, a directly observed post-restart boot-identity change, and -- notably for node1 -- a genuinely observed disruption (the ACL service failed at boot due to an nftables table race, leaving the FORWARD chain empty) followed by a diagnosed fix and confirmed restoration, which is a stronger and more convincing recovery demonstration than a simple restart/reconfirm cycle. The fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshot's boot IDs match the executor's own final observations for all three nodes, corroborating the restart trace. The one blemish is an unexplained newly-failed system-health.service on node1 post-restart, which was not investigated.
limitations: Only ICMP was used to represent 'rest of forwarded traffic'; other protocols/ports besides 8080, 23, and ICMP were not tested.
A new failed unit (system-health.service) appears on node1 in the after-executor snapshot relative to before-prepare, with no executor investigation or explanation captured.
Restart/persistence was not part of the literal task instruction, so its evidence quality affects confidence and hygiene but does not gate the three material outcomes above.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor actions were largely read-only diagnostics or purposeful configuration/cleanup. One diagnostic tcpdump capture to /tmp/e1.pcap on node1 (cmd-14b492bbc66141ad) was started for ARP/neighbor troubleshooting unrelated to the final solution and later killed (cmd-220dc660b5a24b76); the file does not appear in the after-executor temp-file inventory, so it left no residue. Temporary nc listeners on node2/node3 were reliably cleaned up after each test round (cmd-0e8e71a0a66f43fd, cmd-d6d056e76d6e426c, cmd-2cc617fd0ab44448). The persistence mechanism (systemd oneshot service + 60s self-healing timer) is a reasonable, bounded implementation choice for surviving caclmgrd's dynamic nftables table recreation. One notable open item: the after-executor lifecycle snapshot shows a new failed unit, system-health.service, on node1 that was not present in the before-prepare baseline and was not investigated or explained by the executor after the reboot sequence -- this is unaddressed residue from the executor-performed restart and should be flagged rather than ignored.
